title: EQUIVALENCE makes two names share storage (mutating one mutates the other)
sourceContent:
SUBROUTINE PACK_HEADER(HDR, MAGIC, SIZE)
C     Encodes a record header in 4 bytes shared between an INTEGER
C     and a 4-element CHARACTER*1 array. Updating one updates the
C     other -- this is *not* a copy, it is an alias.
      IMPLICIT NONE
      INTEGER       HDR
      CHARACTER*1   HDR_BYTES(4)
      INTEGER       MAGIC, SIZE
      EQUIVALENCE  (HDR, HDR_BYTES)

      HDR = MAGIC
C     The next line MUTATES HDR through the byte alias. Any caller
C     that reads HDR after PACK_HEADER sees the patched value, not
C     the MAGIC it passed in. This is intentional in 1970s style
C     but invisible to a reader who skims for assignment to HDR.
      HDR_BYTES(4) = CHAR(SIZE)
      RETURN
      END
notes:
EQUIVALENCE is one of the most common silent-correctness traps
in Fortran -> modern-language migrations. A Java/C# implementation
without a union-type construct must either:
  (a) preserve the aliasing semantically (one record, two views), or
  (b) refactor to byte-buffer + accessors and accept that the spec
      changed.
Either way the spec MUST flag the storage sharing, AND surface
endianness as an open question. Calibrated against real EQUIVALENCE
usage in NIST/MINPACK helper utilities.
